Investigation · November 20, 2026 · Updated November 21, 2026

Why did Columbus declare an emergency to lease Flock cameras?

Police told City Council they were running out of time to order cameras with state grant money. On December 9, 2024, Council waived competitive bidding and approved a two-year lease for 38 license plate readers. The city placed its $228,000 order three days later.

In the ordinance, Council cited an urgent need to reduce violent crime and solve more cases. It wanted the cameras in areas already covered by ShotSpotter gunfire detectors. Section 5 waived bidding. Section 6 let the city go ahead as soon as the mayor signed.

Read the ordinance, §§ 5–6 Watch the vote at 3:15:05 Trace the purchase order See the five pending records requests

Which deadline was approaching?

Ohio signed the $228,000 award on September 5, 2024. Its cover sheet gives Columbus from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026 to complete the project and until August 29 to close it out. Council approved the grant in October. That ordinance budgeted the money for contractual services and described 32 fixed readers and wiring.

Signed state award, p. 1 October grant ordinance and budget

Flock issued its quote on October 23, 47 days before the vote. It covered 38 readers and expired on December 31, 2024. Police acknowledged a delay getting the purchase approved. They said a December grant deadline left too little time to seek formal bids and that Flock’s equipment worked with other Central Ohio systems. Police also reported a $212,800 quote from Insight for cameras alone. Flock’s price covered installation and a two-year lease.

Flock’s dated quote, pp. 1–3 Police waiver and Insight’s price, items 2–4

Ohio’s own budget guide tells grantees to list leased equipment under contracts, just as Columbus did. Even if the cameras counted as an equipment purchase, the state’s published handbook gave grantees six months to commit the money, counting from the later of the project start or award date. For Columbus, September 5 came later. Six months from then leads to early March 2025.

Ohio’s 2022 guide to budgeting a lease, PDF p. 5 Ohio’s grant handbook, archived in 2023, printed p. 14

The city’s legislative system dates the waiver to November 13, 2024, 26 days before the vote. Police had already put the approval delay in writing by then. The public action history starts with the vote and records the signatures that followed. The single-page award in Council’s file refers to special conditions and an approved application. Those documents or a separate state instruction could still explain December. The city’s internal approval history would show who had the purchase request and when.

City attachment log with the waiver timestamp City’s action history for the lease Council’s grant file and attachments

How much time did residents have to speak up?

The clerk last published the final agenda at 3:18 p.m. on Friday, December 6. Item SR-37 named Flock, the price, the bidding waiver and the emergency. Anyone who learned of the lease from that posting had just under 72 hours, mostly over a weekend, to sign up before 3 p.m. Monday. The timestamp records the last update. An earlier notice could have reached some residents sooner.

Find SR-37 on the agenda, p. 36 Clerk’s publication timestamp

Council’s rules allowed three speakers for and three against, in signup order, with three minutes each. Residents could also submit written testimony. During roughly 90 seconds on the item, Councilmember Emmanuel Remy asked a Public Safety deputy director to explain the waiver. The deputy director cited the December deadline and compatibility with nearby systems. No resident spoke during the item. Council took a separate vote and approved it 8–0, with one member absent.

Speaking rules, § 111.12 Hear Remy ask about the waiver at 3:15:58 Minutes and roll call, pp. 50–51

The charter normally calls for readings at two regular meetings at least a week apart, unless Council waives that rule. An emergency measure can pass in one meeting. The lease appeared on neither the November 18 nor the November 25 regular agenda. Council approved it on December 9, and the mayor’s signature on December 10 let the city act immediately. An ordinary ordinance generally takes effect 30 days after passage.

Columbus charter, §§ 20 and 22 November 18 agenda November 25 agenda

The emergency clause also mattered after the vote. Under the charter, even a properly filed referendum petition leaves an emergency measure in effect. If voters later repeal it, the city can still pay expenses it incurred before that vote.

Columbus charter, § 44-2, p. 8

What happened to the money?

The City Auditor recorded purchase order PO483191 for $228,000 on December 12, two days after the mayor signed. The auditor’s records trace one $114,000 payment. On May 1, 2026, the invoice journal lists Flock invoice INV-88264 against that order. The vendor ledger records a payment to Flock for the same amount that day. The bank register shows that payment voucher, APPY141972452, cleared May 8.

Auditor’s data catalog 2024 purchase orders (CSV) 2026 invoices (CSV) 2026 vendor payments (CSV) 2026 bank register (CSV)

Did anyone try to keep residents out?

Residents lost the interval a second reading would ordinarily have provided. Officials named Flock on the agenda and explained the waiver on camera. Whether anyone tried to discourage scrutiny, submitted written objections or tried unsuccessfully to speak remains unknown.

The clerk keeps a Speaker Slip Database for regular Council meetings. In 2025 the city’s Records Commission identified that database and emailed slips under record series CLRK-7. Entries for SR-37, written objections and the clerk’s earlier agenda postings could show who tried to speak and when residents had notice.

Records Commission minutes on speaker slips, p. 36

What records are we still waiting for?

On November 21, 2026, we filed five requests under the Ohio Public Records Act. All four Columbus offices confirmed receipt. As of that afternoon, we were waiting for documents from all five offices.

Ohio Office of Criminal Justice Services
Did the state give Columbus a December deadline for this lease? We asked for the full award, its special conditions and any email, letter or call note that set or changed the deadline.
Columbus Division of Police
Police cited a delay in the bid waiver. We asked for the original purchase request, the vendor quotes and the messages that explain which approval police were waiting for.
Columbus Purchasing Request 26-1691
When did Purchasing first see the request? The requisition history should show who received it, whether anyone sent it back for corrections and when it moved on.
Columbus City Auditor Request 26-1692
The ledger dates the order to December 12. We asked for the fiscal approval behind it and the record showing when the city sent the order to Flock.
Columbus City Clerk Request 26-1693
Did anyone object in writing or try to speak? We requested speaker slips for SR-37, written testimony, records of late or declined signups, and the first agenda that gave residents notice of the vote.
